extracted.intended_audience: policy-makers, administrative law officials, tribunal designers, legal scholars, and administrators of social security programs
extracted.subtask_short: designing administrative procedure for social security
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for structuring administrative procedure and appeals in the federal social security sector (CPP, unemployment insurance, family allowances, Old Age Security), including objectives, procedural safeguards, information access, tribunal design, and adaptations for high-volume benefit litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile public interest and individual safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential purpose of administrative procedure is to reconcile the requirements of the public interest with the necessary safeguards for individual interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure should both serve the public interest (efficient, well-informed decision-making) and protect the legitimate rights and interests of individuals (equity, participation, remedies). This dual imperative underpins all subsequent specific proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure decision-maker is fully informed
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions require that the decision-maker be correctly and fully informed: the administrative authority must be in possession of all the facts relevant to the problem, drawn from the persons affected, third-party informants, and standards or data originating with the authority itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The informing process includes gathering, finding and evaluation of facts by the initial decision-maker and transmission of results to subsequent decision-making authorities; see section III for more on methods of informing the decision-maker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedite decision-making / promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative procedure ought to contribute to expediting the treatment of matters rather than delaying them; speed is essential both at initial decision and appellate levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules should avoid 'lawyer's artifices' that merely postpone outcomes; speed is particularly critical in social security because of claimants' economic needs. Section V addresses speed in more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assure execution and enforcement of decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective administrative decisions must be actually executed: in contributions this means assessed amounts must be collected and transmitted; for benefits it means recovery of illegal payments and deployment of sanctions where misconduct is wilful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural arrangements must include mechanisms to effect recovery and sanctions and handle enforcement-related procedural problems; enforcement will be discussed in section VII.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informing individuals of reasons, rights, and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals want to understand the reasons for administrative actions, be informed of their rights and recourses, means of redress, and scope of obligations; initial contacts and written reasons are important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrations should give access to information before involvement, explain conduct of proceedings, tell claimants what is expected of them, provide written reasons for decisions affecting them, and ensure access to legislation, regulations and caselaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable effective public participation in decision-making (convergent procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens should be associated with the decision-making process through participation that lets them express their view and contribute to the decision affecting their interests—termed a 'convergent procedure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access requirements include access to the administrative authority and decision-maker (in person where feasible), access to the file, and machinery for ongoing input in matters where cooperation continues after decision (e.g., benefit administration). Fairness requires litigation procedures that allow a real possibility of making views prevail before review authorities; section IV treats participation in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible, impartial, and technically competent review authority
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be an avenue of appeal that is easy to access, requires minimal formality, is impartial, technically competent, and produces decisions of high quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An administrative tribunal is normally preferable to superior courts for reasons of cost, speed and technical specialization; the structure and organization of the review authority should enhance impartiality and competence (see section VI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and development of precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Social security's egalitarian character calls for consistency: identical cases should be treated uniformly, and decision-makers should establish standards and conserve precedents to ensure uniformity over time and across locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency argues for administrative organization that issues standards, maintains internal precedents, and ideally a single appeal authority of last resort which can construct an authoritative caselaw accessible to administration and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design procedures for high-volume, repetitive social security cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Because social security involves myriads of isolated and repetitive decisions in varied combinations, procedures must address both efficiency and equity to ensure justice in millions of individual cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative arrangements should enable adequate information, participation, and appeal mechanisms on a mass scale; organizational solutions (uniform methods, planning, staff handbooks) help manage volume while protecting fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize speed due to claimant vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: The dire economic plight of claimants demands speedy determinations; excessive delay defeats social security's purpose to help citizens in distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural rules should aim to minimize delay in benefit allocation and in contribution assessments; the need for promptness is heightened by the financial consequences for claimants and fund administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt procedural tone: non-adversarial for benefits, adversarial for contributions where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative action in benefit claims generally occurs in a non-adversary, humanitarian atmosphere and this should be maintained; by contrast, contribution-related proceedings resemble tax litigation and may require more adversarial procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures should preserve the cooperative, humane atmosphere for benefits (especially pensions and disability) while allowing more formal, adversarial processes in controversies over contributions that involve contracts, corporate law, labour relations, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor procedures to predominance of disability-pension cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Disability-pension cases constitute the lion's share of the Board's workload (e.g., 71% of appeals and 83% of CPP-related appeals in cited period), so procedural proposals should focus primarily on this branch of litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rules, resources and tribunal specializations with disability claims' factual and evidentiary features in mind; recognize that many recommendations will be shaped by this workload composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation into a single federal social security tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrate litigation arising out of all federal social security programmes before a single, permanent and specialized administrative tribunal with final appeal jurisdiction to achieve individualized justice, consistency and rapidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed Federal Social Security Tribunal would succeed current specialized fora (unemployment insurance umpire, PAB, Review Committees) and cover CPP, unemployment insurance, family allowances, Old Age Security, and possibly veterans' pensions; section VI sketches structure and operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure public access to intelligible legal rules and caselaw
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimants need access to the Act, regulations and caselaw that define rights and eligibility; statutes and regulations should be intelligible to the average citizen or translated into plain language by manuals, forms, directives and circulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation offered by offices should do more than paraphrase ambiguous statutory terms; citizens (and their representatives) must have ready access to substantive law and procedural regulations so they can assess chances of success and participate meaningfully in proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use uniform procedural methods and administrative handbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing uniform methods and procedural handbooks facilitates and accelerates administrative work, aids planning, simplifies public relations and fosters administrative efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardized practices help ensure consistent answers to identical questions and support the conservation of precedents; they also assist officials in applying complex statutory language in day-to-day operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize appellate levels; ensure prompt transmission to final authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless justified, multiplicity of appeal levels should be abolished to reduce delay; cases should reach the final appeal authority promptly to enable rulings within a minimum of delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamlined appellate structure promotes speedy final resolution for contributors and beneficiaries; organizational and procedural measures should aim to reduce intermediate layers that prolong litigation.
